Where the praise is to be offered divides them from the first line. Ellicott takes the sanctuary for the temple and reads the psalm as moving from earth to heaven, reversing the order of the psalm before it. Clarke allows the temple, any place dedicated to God's service, or else his holiness, meaning his holy influence in the heart; he takes the firmament for the whole expanse and asks the inhabitants of all those worlds to join the chorus. Wesley divides neatly: the sanctuary is the temple, the firmament heaven, and there let the blessed angels praise him. Calvin rejects precisely that reading as forced and unnatural. Heaven is meant in both clauses, he holds, the second merely repeating the first, the point being to make men lift their eyes toward the heavenly sanctuary, the heavens being a mirror of God's greatness. Delitzsch agrees that both terms are attributive to God and name what is heavenly. Henry sets out both without choosing, and finds comfort in the second: when we do this work poorly here, it is done far better there.

The counting and the instruments draw out the technicians. Delitzsch records that the synagogue reckoned thirteen divine attributes and that Kimchi matched them to thirteen imperatives here, but thinks the tenfold call enclosed between the Hallelujahs likelier to be the significant figure, ten being the number of completeness. Clarke notes this is the first place where the compound is praise God rather than praise the Lord, and Spurgeon builds on the same change of names: power is joined to holiness, since power without righteousness would be oppression and righteousness without power too weak to be useful. Clarke works through the instruments one by one: a horn named from its majestic sound, a hollow stringed instrument he likens to a guitar, a drum stretched over a broad hoop, strings shortening to a point, which a manuscript Psalter on his desk pictures David playing, and a mouth organ of seven canes. He insists flatly that the word rendered dance is a pipe and never means dance. Ellicott covers the same ground more cautiously, rendering one word simply as strings, listing three rival identifications of the organ, and noting the two cymbals distinguished as of hearing and of tumult.

Henry will not have the question matter. It is well, he says, that we need not enquire what these instruments were; the passage teaches that in serving God we should spare no cost, and that the best music in God's ears is devout affection, not a melodious string but a melodious heart. On the greatness to be praised he warns against the opposite error from the usual one: we cannot speak of God hyperbolically, and the danger lies all in saying too little. Gill reads the mighty acts as creation, providence, redemption and grace together.

The last verse is where the sharpest disagreement falls. Delitzsch takes the call, addressed to Israel so far by implication of the instrument names, as generalized now to the totality of breath, and hears the Psalter close on that full-toned finale. Henry canvasses both senses, allowing that the singing of birds is a kind of praise and that the brutes in effect ask men to do it for them; Gill and Wesley take it as wide as it goes. Clarke reads it as a stage direction, all voices and instruments summoned to close the service in full chorus. Ellicott resists the instinct: we naturally wish the words their largest intent, but the psalm places us so positively inside the temple among the covenant people that only those assembled there can be meant, and the closing hallelujah rises from Hebrew voices alone. Augustine is occupied elsewhere, reading the number of the psalms as a multiple of fifteen, which he makes the concord of the two Testaments, the Sabbath being the seventh day and the Lord's Day the eighth.
